what_its_for: Alcohol is used as an antiseptic to clean and disinfect skin before injections, blood draws, or minor procedures. It kills germs on the surface of the skin. Alcohol gel or liquid is also used as a hand sanitizer to reduce the spread of bacteria and viruses. In rare medical settings, a doctor may prescribe a special form of alcohol to treat certain poisonings or to destroy nerve tissue near tumors.
how_to_take: For skin cleaning: Wipe the area firmly with an alcohol swab or cotton ball soaked in alcohol. Rub for at least 15 to 30 seconds and let it air dry completely before the injection or procedure. Do not blow on it or fan it dry. For hand sanitizer: Apply a dime-sized amount to your palm, rub your hands together covering all surfaces including between fingers and under nails, and keep rubbing until your hands feel dry (about 20 seconds). Do not rinse off. For medical-grade alcohol injections: Only a trained healthcare provider will give this type of treatment.
dosing: Skin antiseptic: Use one swab or enough liquid to thoroughly wet the area each time you need it. Hand sanitizer: Use one pump or about 1 to 2 mL each time you sanitize your hands. Repeat after touching dirty surfaces, before eating, or after using the bathroom. There is no set number of times per day, but use it as often as needed to keep hands clean. Medical-grade injections: Dosed and given only by your doctor.
missed_dose: Alcohol is not taken on a regular dosing schedule like a daily medication, so there is no missed dose to worry about. Simply use it the next time you need to clean your skin or sanitize your hands.
storage: Store alcohol products at room temperature, away from heat, open flames, and direct sunlight, as alcohol is flammable. Keep the cap tightly closed when not in use to prevent evaporation. Keep out of reach of children. Do not store near stoves, candles, or fireplaces. Check the expiration date on the label and do not use expired products.
what_to_avoid: Do not use alcohol on open wounds, deep cuts, or serious burns, as it can damage tissue and slow healing. Do not use near open flames or while smoking, since alcohol is highly flammable. Avoid getting alcohol in your eyes, mouth, or nose. Do not swallow hand sanitizer or rubbing alcohol, as this is extremely dangerous and can cause serious harm or death, especially in children. Do not use large amounts on a baby's skin. Avoid using alcohol-based hand sanitizers if you have a true allergy to alcohol.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if: a child swallows hand sanitizer or rubbing alcohol, you develop signs of alcohol poisoning such as confusion, vomiting, difficulty breathing, or loss of consciousness, you have a severe skin reaction such as blistering, severe redness, or swelling after using an alcohol product, or you develop signs of infection at a site that was cleaned with alcohol, such as increasing redness, warmth, pus, or fever.
when_it_works: As a skin antiseptic, alcohol works almost immediately, killing most germs on the skin surface within 15 to 30 seconds. As a hand sanitizer, it reduces germs on your hands right away, within about 20 to 30 seconds of rubbing your hands together. Keep in mind that alcohol does not work as well if your hands are visibly dirty or greasy, so wash with soap and water first in those cases.
special_populations: Children: Keep all alcohol products out of reach of children. Even small amounts of swallowed alcohol can be very dangerous for young children and can cause dangerously low blood sugar and breathing problems. Use alcohol-based products on children's skin only as directed. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Topical use of alcohol on the skin is generally considered safe. Avoid excessive skin application. Elderly patients: Safe to use on skin as directed. Be cautious around open flames if using flammable alcohol products. People with sensitive skin: May experience dryness or irritation with frequent use. Consider using a moisturizer after repeated use of hand sanitizer.
